title: Plates on the Move
welcome_lead: Welcome, young geographer! Earth's surface is broken into giant slabs called tectonic plates. Today you will explore how they move and shape our world.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Earth's crust is split into 7 large plates and many smaller ones. They float on the hot, semi-liquid mantle below.

These plates move only a few centimetres a year, about the speed your fingernails grow!

• Constructive: plates move apart (e.g. Mid-Atlantic Ridge).
  • Destructive: plates collide; one is forced down (e.g. west coast of South America).
  • Conservative: plates slide past each other (e.g. San Andreas Fault).
Plate movement causes earthquakes, volcanoes and even tsunamis. Where plates meet, danger often follows.

Sand moves along the beach because tides pull it sideways.
Lag time is the delay between thunder and lightning.
The zigzag movement of sediment along a coast caused by waves approaching at an angle (swash up the beach) and gravity returning water perpendicular (backwash).
Longshore drift is the rising of sea level over time.

mcqs.q: How do scientists know current climate change is anthropogenic?
options: Climate change is caused by the sun getting hotter.
Isotopic signatures of CO2 match fossil fuel sources, warming patterns (cooler stratosphere, warmer troposphere) match greenhouse forcing, and natural forcings cannot explain the rate.
Longshore drift is the rising of sea level over time.
Climate change is mainly caused by natural Milankovitch cycles.
